content.text:
Plan a story of about 2800 words from this premise.

Write a first-person detective story featuring a locked-room murder case in 2800 words. The story should be tightly plotted with strong suspense.

Propose about 4 scenes of roughly 700 words each. Give every character, location and significant object a stable id now — later scenes can only refer to entities that exist. State the world rules the story must not break. Then call submit_plan.

entities.sketch: First-person narrator and private investigator (mid-40s). Ex-detective turned PI; wry, exacting, easily bored. Keeps careful notes and narrates events in present-tense memory with professional reserve and a private grief that motivates the case.
Victim. Reclusive antiquarian and collector of clocks (late 60s). Owner of Crowe House; meticulous, wealthy, habitually precise about time and keys.
Edmund's niece (early 30s). Smart, urbane, outwardly calm; stands to inherit if Edmund dies without a will change. Says she was at a dinner party across town the night of the murder.
Long-time housekeeper and caretaker for Crowe House (50s). Quiet, loyal, knows the mansion's quirks and maintenance secrets. Says he discovered the body and called the police.
Neighbor and fellow collector (40s). Friendly rivalry with Edmund over rare pieces; arrives later that evening claiming he went to borrow a book and found the road blocked.
Medical examiner assigned to the case. Direct, clinical; concise about time and cause of death in ways that tighten the timeline rather than loosen it.
Local police inspector. Professional, courteous to the narrator but territorial. Ran the initial scene and left the room sealed until the coroner finished.

The locked room. A compact, wood-paneled study on the ground floor at the rear of Crowe House. Heavy oak door with an old brass lock; single sash window with an internal latch; desk faces the window; mantel with an antique clock above it.
Entrance hall and route to the study. Wide, shadowed in the evening; coat hooks and a front door that is often left unlocked for guests.
An ornate mantel clock Edmund prized. It had stopped at 2:17 when the body was found. The clock is mechanical and old; it can be wound and its casing hides a shallow false back.
Small brass skeleton key of the old oak lock on the study door. At discovery the official record notes the study's door was locked from the inside and the key was not in the lock.
A torn piece of stationery found in Edmund's right hand; fragment contains a few words in a tight, nervous hand and an ink blot. The rest of the letter is missing when the scene is first examined.
An antique bottle of iron gall ink kept on Edmund's desk. Labeled and dusty; a thin ring of dried ink sits on its lip. It is a plausible medium for a poisonous application if tampered with.
The internal latch on the study's sash window. Appears undisturbed on first examination; the sash is latched from the inside and the exterior is unreachable without a ladder.
A single set of muddy bootprints on the flagstone path leading to the rear of the house; recorded in the initial scene log. Patterned, large, possibly from work boots.

arguments.logline: A private investigator called to a sealed study where a reclusive collector has been murdered faces a classic locked-room: door locked from the inside, window latched, clock stopped at the time of death. As interviews and experiments narrow the field, the narrator must outthink an argument that used time and an object meant to order it as a murderer's tool.

scenes.intent: Open on the narrator arriving at Crowe House after the coroner has left. Establish mood (damp evening, exacting eye), present the locked-room puzzle with precise evidence: a study locked from the inside, the antique clock stopped at 2:17, the torn letter in Edmund's hand, key missing from the lock, window latched, a single set of muddy bootprints outside. The narrator records sensory detail, meets Inspector Hart and Omar, and feels the puzzle's shape for the first time.

Close, tense interviews and micro-examinations. The narrator interviews Lydia and Omar separately in the foyer and study; gathers their accounts and watches for breaks. Lydia's alibi has a hole; Omar's hands and shoes have traces that don't match his story. The narrator notices the ink blot and the familiar iron-gall bottle on the desk, and the torn letter's hand is nervous enough to suggest a last-minute confrontation. Dr. Ines Mali's observations tighten the time-of-death window. The narrator begins to sketch a hypothesis involving the clock and the ink bottle.

Experimentation and escalation: the narrator stays past dusk to re-create the locked-room conditions and examine the clock and desk. He manipulates the antique clock (wind, stop, examine false back), tests how a letter could be received and gripped with a poisoned blot, and traces a mechanism (string, pulley or clock-cam) that could have allowed the killer to leave and lock the door from outside. Suspicion shifts from an obvious suspect to a less obvious one as the narrator discovers a small but decisive physical trick involving the clock's false back and the key. Tension rises when a visitor (Daniel Kai) arrives at the gate, unexpected and distracted.

Denouement in which the narrator sets a trap to expose the murderer. He arranges the scene to force a reveal—either by staging the reappearance of the missing letter or by confronting the suspect with a reconstruction that proves access and motive. The reveal ties back to the clock's stopped time, the false back that hid the brass key, and a coerced confession or a flinch that only the guilty can make. Close on the narrator reflecting on the artifice of time, inheritance, and the way ordinary objects can be used to order death.

world_rules: No supernatural explanations: every locked-room solution must be human (mechanical, psychological or misdirection) and physically plausible.
Forensic and timeline details must be internally consistent and match ordinary forensics (time of death windows, temperature effects on a stopped clock are not supernatural).
The narrator is first-person and not omniscient: they do not know other characters' private thoughts unless observed or reported; claims on motive must be supported by evidence in the scenes.
All characters, locations and objects used later will be drawn only from the stable ids declared above; new entities must be added through the plan-update process.
No identifiable real persons or public figures are used or referenced.
